text_chunk: CYP2D6*4 (no function, splice defect rs3892097) is the most common loss-of-function allele in European populations with allele frequency ~20%. Approximately 5-10% of Europeans are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers (most commonly *4/*4), the highest PM prevalence globally. This explains the population-level impact on codeine, tamoxifen, and antidepressant metabolism.

CYP2D6*10 (decreased function, P34S rs1065852) is the most common CYP2D6 variant in East Asian populations with allele frequency ~43%. Most East Asians carry at least one *10 allele, resulting in a high prevalence of intermediate metabolizers (~35-45%). This contributes to different codeine/tramadol dosing requirements in East Asian patients.

CYP2D6*17 (decreased function, T107I rs28371706) is the most common CYP2D6 variant in African populations with allele frequency ~20%. The *17 allele is virtually absent in European and East Asian populations. Many standard CYP2D6 genotyping panels have historically not included *17, leading to misclassification of African patients as normal metabolizers.

CYP2C19*2 (no function, splice defect c.681G>A rs4244285) has the highest frequency in East Asian populations (~30%), compared to ~15% in Europeans and ~15% in Africans. Combined with *3 (~5% in East Asians), approximately 13-23% of East Asians are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers. This has major implications for clopidogrel efficacy in Asian patients undergoing PCI.

CYP2C19*17 (increased function, c.-806C>T rs12248560) is most common in European (~21%) and African (~18%) populations and rare in East Asians (~3%). The *17 allele confers ultra-rapid metabolizer status for clopidogrel (potentially increased efficacy but increased bleeding risk) and PPIs (potentially reduced acid suppression). The high frequency means ~5% of Europeans are CYP2C19 ultra-rapid metabolizers.

CYP2C9*3 (decreased function, I359L rs1057910) has the highest frequency in European populations (~7%), with ~5% in South Asians and <1% in Africans and East Asians. CYP2C9*2 (R144C) is also predominantly found in Europeans (~13%). Together, ~35% of Europeans carry at least one reduced-function CYP2C9 allele, affecting warfarin dosing, phenytoin metabolism, and NSAID clearance.

VKORC1 -1639A allele (rs9923231, warfarin sensitivity) frequency is ~92% in East Asians, ~40% in Europeans, and ~10% in Africans. This explains why East Asian patients typically require warfarin doses of 2-3 mg/day (vs 5 mg/day average in Europeans). The near-fixation of the A allele in East Asians means genotyping provides less discrimination in this population.

DPYD*2A (IVS14+1G>A, no function, rs3918290) has allele frequency ~1.2% in Europeans, ~0.1% in Africans, and is very rare in East Asians. Approximately 3-5% of European patients carry at least one DPYD reduced-function variant when all four CPIC-recommended variants are tested (*2A, *13, D949V, HapB3). Though the carrier rate is low, the severity of fluoropyrimidine toxicity in carriers makes universal pre-treatment testing cost-effective.

NUDT15*3 (R139C, no function, rs116855232) is most prevalent in East Asian populations (~10%), followed by Hispanic/Latino (~4%), South Asian (~3%), and very rare in Europeans (<0.5%) and Africans (<0.5%). In East Asian ALL patients, NUDT15*3 is a stronger predictor of thiopurine-induced leukopenia than TPMT variants, which are rare in this population. This demonstrates the importance of population-appropriate pharmacogenomic panels.

HLA-B*57:01 prevalence is highest in European populations (~6-7%), moderate in South Asian (~2-3%), and low in East Asian (<1%) and African (~1%) populations. Universal screening before abacavir is cost-effective across all populations, including those with low prevalence, because the consequence of an undetected HSR (potential death on rechallenge) is severe. The number needed to genotype to prevent one HSR ranges from ~15 (Europeans) to ~100 (East Asians).

HLA-B*15:02 prevalence varies dramatically within East Asian populations: 8-12% in Southeast Asians (Thai, Malay, Filipino, Vietnamese), 4-6% in Han Chinese, 2-4% in South Asians, and <1% in Europeans, Africans, and Northeast Asians (Japanese, Korean). This allelic heterogeneity requires population-specific screening recommendations — FDA mandates testing only in patients with Asian ancestry.

HLA-B*58:01 prevalence is highest in Korean populations (~12%), followed by other East Asian populations (6-8%), African Americans (3-4%), and Europeans (1-2%). The high Korean prevalence drives the strongly positive cost-effectiveness of pre-allopurinol HLA-B*58:01 screening in this population. South Korea implemented reimbursement for HLA-B*58:01 testing, following Taiwan's successful nationwide program.

SLCO1B1 c.521C allele (rs4149056, V174A, decreased function) has frequency ~15% in Europeans, ~12% in East Asians, ~8% in South Asians, and ~2% in Africans. Approximately 2% of Europeans are CC homozygotes (16.9x myopathy risk with simvastatin). The relatively high heterozygote frequency (~26%) means a substantial proportion of European statin users carry one copy (4.5x myopathy risk). SLCO1B1 genotyping is increasingly incorporated into pre-emptive PGx panels.

CYP3A5*1 (expresser allele, normal function) has dramatically different frequencies across populations: ~70% in Africans, ~25% in East Asians, ~15% in South Asians, and ~6% in Europeans. This means most African individuals are CYP3A5 expressers requiring higher tacrolimus doses, while most Europeans are non-expressers (*3/*3). This population difference contributes to the well-documented higher tacrolimus dose requirements in African American transplant recipients.

G6PD A- variant (V68M+N126D, Class III deficiency) has allele frequency ~20% in sub-Saharan African populations. G6PD deficiency is X-linked, so ~20% of African males are hemizygous (affected). The G6PD Mediterranean variant (S188F, Class II, more severe) is prevalent in Middle Eastern, Southern European, and South Asian populations (~5-15% in males). Worldwide, ~400 million people are G6PD-deficient, making it the most common enzymopathy and a critical pharmacogenomic consideration for primaquine, rasburicase, and dapsone.
